Long-Term Treasury Yields Push Higher Despite Decline in Oil Prices
 
Plus, two-year Treasury yield falls as Fed official signals patience
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
DANIEL HEUER/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Long yields rose again. Yields on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes ticked higher, hitting yet another 19-year high. The 30-year yield rose to 5.594%, its highest level since 2002.

 

The 2-year Treasury yield however fell in afternoon trading. The move may have been prompted by comments from New York Fed President John Williams, who said that the central bank need not rush to continue raising interest rates. Stocks fell slightly, with the Dow closing 0.3% lower while the Nasdaq was down 0.1%.

 

Brent crude futures today gave up some of their recent gains, falling 2.6% to $102.59 a barrel. Oil flows coming out of the Middle East are recovering, which should help ease the energy supply crunch that has dialed up inflationary pressures worldwide.

 

Despite its recent retracement, bitcoin is on pace for its best quarterly performance since the fourth quarter of 2024. It is on track to lock in its first positive quarter in a year, having gained more than 40% from July to September. Higher bond yields, meanwhile, are pushing the dollar higher. The greenback has gained 1.5% against a basket of other currencies this September, following two months of declines.

 
 
 
CONTENT FROM: GOLDMAN SACHS
 
 
The outlook for data center power demand
 
As AI models scale, their massive computational needs are putting unprecedented pressure on power grids. Goldman Sachs Research projects AI will drive an increase of 170% in global data center power demand by 2030, adding the equivalent of Japan's entire electricity consumption.

One Big Story

 
 
MICHAEL NAGLE/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

A top Federal Reserve official suggested Tuesday that the central bank could wait until December before raising interest rates again, pushing back against market bets on a follow-up increase next month. 

 

The remarks from New York Fed President John Williams carry particular weight because as vice chair of the Fed’s rate-setting committee, he has typically sought to reflect the views of the committee’s center of gravity rather than stake out his own position.
